chunks: Muhammad ibn Musa ibn al-Mutevakil (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Ali ibn al-Hussein al-Sa'ed Abady quoted on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Abu Ahmad Muhammad ibn Zyad al-Azdi that he had heard the jurisprudent in Medina Malik ibn Anas say:

I used to visit Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon them both), and he would present me with a cushion and show me respect, saying, 'O Malik, I love you.' I would keep this to myself and praise God for it. He (peace be upon him) was never without one of three states: either fasting, standing in prayer, or remembering God. He was among the greatest of worshippers and the most eminent of ascetics who feared God, the Exalted. He was a man of much speech, pleasant in company, and abundant in beneficial knowledge. Whenever he mentioned, 'The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said,' his face would turn blue one time and yellow another, until those who knew him could hardly recognize him. I performed Hajj with him once. When his mount was settled for the Ihram, whenever he was about to say the Talbiyah, his voice would cut off in his throat, and he nearly fell from his mount. I said, 'Say, O son of the Messenger of God, for you must say it.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'O Ibn Abi Amer, how can I dare to say, "Here I am, O God, here I am," when I fear that the Exalted and Mighty One might respond to me, "Not here you are, nor your happiness"?'

key_terms.التَّلْبِيَة: Talbiyah (the invocation during Hajj: Labbayk Allahumma Labbayk)
key_terms.الصَّادِقُ: Al-Sadiq (the Truthful), a title for Imam Ja'far ibn Muhammad
key_terms.الْإِحْرَام: Ihram (the state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah)

ai.seo_question: What were the three constant states of Imam al-Sadiq (as) and why did he hesitate to say Talbiyah during Hajj?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Khisal highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (as) triad of perpetual worship—fasting, standing, and remembrance—reflecting the Shia emphasis on the integration of spiritual asceticism with scholarly engagement. The account of his hesitation during the Talbiyah, fearing divine rejection, underscores the concept of *khawf* (awe) even for the Infallibles, a key theme in Shia hagiography. His close interaction with Malik ibn Anas, the founder of the Maliki school, also illustrates the cross-sectarian respect and transmission of knowledge between the Ahl al-Bayt and the broader Muslim scholarly community.
